analysis.one_liner: Requires companies and data brokers to protect personal data, notify people of breaches, and let them fix their files.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill on November 17, 2005, and placed it on the Senate calendar, but it never came up for a floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required companies holding sensitive personal data on 10,000 or more Americans to build real security programs with encryption, access controls, and testing, and to tell people quickly when their data is breached. It would have given individuals the right to see the records data brokers keep on them and force corrections of errors, and it would have made concealing a breach a federal crime. It also would have forced federal agencies to assess privacy impacts before buying personal data from brokers. It cleared the Judiciary Committee on a favorable report but was never brought to the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans whose names, Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, and health information sit in corporate and government databases. Breach victims would learn quickly what happened and what to do; people profiled by data brokers could see and correct the files sold about them; identity theft victims could get extended fraud alerts on their credit files.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose personal data is held by companies

how_it_helps.text: Requires any agency or business that suffers a security breach involving sensitive personal data to notify affected residents without unreasonable delay, including what information was taken and a toll-free number for help.
Gives individuals the right to obtain, for a reasonable fee, all records a data broker maintains on them for sale to third parties, plus a published process to dispute and correct inaccuracies.

Requires businesses holding sensitive data on 10,000 or more Americans to implement a comprehensive security program: risk assessments, access controls, encryption, regular testing, employee training, and safe disposal of data and hardware.

Makes it a federal crime to conceal a security breach and makes fraud involving unauthorized access to personal data a predicate offense under the RICO organized-crime law, with the Sentencing Commission directed to stiffen identity-theft sentencing guidelines.
Authorizes the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general to enforce the bill with daily civil penalties against violators.
Requires federal agencies to complete a privacy impact assessment before buying personal data from data brokers, and directs the Comptroller General to audit agency use of commercial databases.
Amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act so consumers who receive notice their financial data was compromised qualify for an extended fraud alert on their credit files.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and any business entity in interstate commerce holding sensitive personal data on 10,000 or more Americans would bear the cost of building security programs, encrypting data, and sending breach notifications, and would face daily civil penalties for violations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and large data-holding companies

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly creates no private right of action, so an individual harmed by a data broker's practices could not sue on their own; enforcement would rest entirely on the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general.

A risk-assessment exemption lets a company avoid notifying anyone if it tells the Secret Service there is no significant risk of harm and the Secret Service does not object within 10 days, putting the judgment call largely in the company's hands.

Companies with fraud-blocking security programs are exempt from notification for breaches involving only account numbers, and law enforcement can delay public notice, both of which narrow the right to know.
The data broker title preempts state laws on access to and correction of broker records, so states could not impose stronger rules in that area.
Businesses would bear real compliance costs for security programs, encryption, testing, and notification, and these costs would be largest for companies holding data on millions of people.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are substantial and aimed at a real, widespread harm: identity theft affected millions of Americans a year by the bill's own findings. The costs fall on companies as compliance and notification expenses, which is the point of deterrence. The design weaknesses are genuine: no right to sue, a self-serving risk-assessment exemption, and preemption of some state rules. On balance this was a serious consumer-protection bill whose main gap was leaving enforcement to government agencies rather than victims.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it and put it on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but Senate leaders never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Arlen Specter, a Republican and chairman of the Judiciary Committee, introduced the bill on September 29, 2005, joined by Democratic Senators Leahy, Feinstein, and Feingold.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which held markup sessions on October 20 and October 27, 2005.
On November 17, 2005, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and Senator Specter reported it to the Senate.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 297, the waiting list for bills ready for floor action.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a Senate floor vote and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the companies holding Americans' personal records are better off: no federal breach-notification, security-program, or data-broker disclosure law took effect, and they avoided the compliance costs and penalties. Consumers were left with a patchwork of state breach-notification laws instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and companies holding consumer data

sides.party_line_note: A Republican committee chairman introduced and reported the bill with three Democratic cosponsors, and no floor vote was ever held that would have shown a party split.

industries.note: The bill would force brokers selling sensitive personal data on 5,000 or more people to let individuals see and correct the records sold about them, and face FTC and state enforcement with civil penalties. This strikes directly at a business model built on trading personal information without the subject's knowledge.

industries.industry: Credit bureaus, financial institutions, and HIPAA-covered health entities
industries.note: These already-regulated industries are exempt from the new data-broker and security rules because they are covered by the Fair Credit Reporting Act, Gramm-Leach-Bliley, and HIPAA, and the data broker title preempts states from adding stricter access-and-correction rules. That locks in the existing regulatory channels as the ceiling.

industries.industry: Companies holding consumer data (retailers, employers, government contractors)
industries.note: Any business handling sensitive data on 10,000 or more Americans would have to build security programs with encryption and testing and notify people of breaches, bearing compliance and notification costs. Consumers gain protections in the same transaction, so the industry's cost is the public's benefit.

Agencies would face the same breach-notification duties as companies, plus privacy impact assessments and audits before buying personal data from brokers, and the Justice Department would need a Chief Privacy Officer. This subjects government data handling to the same scrutiny as corporate handling.
